item.title: How Long Should You Do Box Breathing For? From 1 Minute to 5
item.description: How long should you do box breathing for? About 1 minute (4 rounds) takes the edge off. 5 minutes is a fuller reset. Rounds, research, and safety.
item.content:encoded:
How long should you do box breathing for? For a quick reset, four rounds of 4-4-4-4 is enough, and that takes about one minute. For a fuller reset, aim for about five minutes. As a habit, once or twice a day is a common recommendation. Short sessions count.

Most guides bury a single number ("a few minutes," "three to four rounds") somewhere near the bottom. The more useful answer depends on why you're doing it, so below we break it down by situation, then cover the research and how to tell when you can stop.

The quick math: how long one round of box breathing takes

Box breathing is a paced breathing technique: you breathe in for a count of four, hold for four, breathe out for four and hold again for four, tracing the four sides of a box. One trip around the box is one round.

At one second per count, one round takes 16 seconds. That makes the numbers simple:

  • 4 rounds: about 64 seconds
  • 8 rounds: about 2 minutes
  • 18 to 19 rounds: about 5 minutes

If you'd rather not count, the free box breathing timer paces the 4-4-4-4 pattern for you. Stop after four rounds for a one-minute reset, or let it run for about five minutes for a longer session.

How many rounds of box breathing should you do?

Four rounds is the most common answer, and it's a good default for calming down in the moment. Cleveland Clinic suggests three to four rounds, and both University of Minnesota Extension and RWJBarnabas Health suggest four. A University of Michigan handout goes a bit longer, suggesting at least five boxes, and says you can start with a count of 2 or 3.

Situation Rounds (4-4-4-4) Time What it's for
Mid-scroll reset 4 About 1 minute Taking the edge off after a feed has wound you up
Fuller reset 18 to 19 About 5 minutes When one minute took the edge off but you want to settle further
Daily practice 4 to 19 1 to 5 minutes, once or twice a day Making the technique familiar so it's easy to reach for
Winding down at night 4 to 8, with gentler counts 1 to 2 minutes A quiet transition toward bed

These sources don't really disagree. Three or four rounds is sized for a single stressful moment, and five or more minutes is closer to a practice session. None of these numbers come from a trial that compared different lengths of box breathing, so treat them as sensible starting points rather than prescribed doses.

Is 1 minute of box breathing enough?

For taking the edge off a stressful moment, one minute may well be enough. In a 2026 preregistered pilot study of 47 students, one minute of box breathing during real anxious moments in daily life reduced state anxiety more than a passive control, measured five minutes later. One minute of cyclic sighing did too.

Keep that result in proportion, though. It's a small pilot study in students, and what we can report comes from the study's abstract. It suggests a short session can help in the moment. It doesn't show that one minute is the ideal length, or that it works for everyone.

The same study also found slower reaction times after both breathing exercises. The authors called this unexpected, and box breathing was also linked to fewer inhibition errors, especially in participants with higher trait anxiety. Either way, it's sensible to give yourself a short pause before anything that needs quick reactions, such as driving.

Box breathing mid-scroll: a 60-second script

Here's the moment we have in mind. You picked up your phone to check one thing. Twenty minutes later your jaw is tight, your shoulders are up near your ears, and you feel oddly wired for someone who has been sitting still. That's the feed doing what feeds do, and it's a good time for four rounds. (We explain why it happens in nervous system overload from your phone.)

  1. Put the phone face down, or turn the screen off.
  2. Breathe out fully so you start the box empty.
  3. Breathe in gently through your nose for 4.
  4. Hold for 4, keeping your throat and shoulders soft rather than clamped.
  5. Breathe out slowly for 4.
  6. Hold, empty, for 4.
  7. Repeat for four rounds. Tap one finger against your thumb at the end of each round so you don't have to keep count in your head.
  8. Let your breathing go back to normal for a couple of breaths and notice how you feel.

That's it. You can stop at four rounds. If you'd like something to follow, open the box breathing timer and stop it after about a minute.

DeRot is built for this mid-scroll moment. It pauses your apps while you reset with a few calming breaths, so the wired feeling can fade before you go back to the feed. It's coming soon to iOS.

What does a 5-minute session do? What the Stanford study found

The best-known study of box breathing used five-minute sessions: a 2023 Stanford randomized trial in which 108 people spent five minutes a day for 28 days on mindfulness meditation or on one of several breathing practices, including box breathing and cyclic sighing. Twenty-one people were assigned to box breathing.

Here's what it found:

  • Positive mood went up in the box breathing group, but only cyclic sighing significantly beat mindfulness on positive mood.
  • State anxiety fell in every group, including mindfulness, with no significant differences between groups.
  • Across the breathing groups as a whole, gains in positive mood grew with the number of days people practiced. The paper doesn't report this for box breathing on its own.
  • There was no significant change in heart rate variability (HRV) or resting heart rate.

On HRV, the broader picture is more encouraging. A 2022 review of 223 studies found that slow breathing in general increased vagally mediated HRV during sessions, right after them, and over multiple sessions. That hasn't been shown for box breathing specifically, so we wouldn't promise it.

The Stanford study was exploratory, and each technique had a small group. Its results suggest that five minutes of daily box breathing may lift mood and ease anxiety without clearly beating mindfulness meditation, and that across the breathing groups, practicing on more days went with bigger mood gains. That's a long way from headlines about a five-minute breathing trick to "kill stress instantly". The evidence describes a modest, gentle effect, not an off switch.

How do you know when you can stop?

You can stop once the edge is gone, even if that's before your planned number of rounds. We haven't found research that pins down a stopping point for box breathing, so these cues come from experience rather than studies:

  • Your breath starts to slow and deepen on its own, and the counts feel easy rather than effortful.
  • Your jaw unclenches and your shoulders drop.
  • The urge to keep counting fades, and you can think about what's next without a jolt.

If you've done four rounds and still feel wound up, do four more, or switch to a pattern with a longer exhale. Beyond that, more minutes aren't automatically better. Box breathing is a way back to baseline, not an endurance event.

What if 4-second holds feel like too much?

Shorten the counts. Box breathing works at whatever length lets you breathe without strain. Four seconds is a convention, not a rule.

  • 3-3-3-3: 12-second rounds, five rounds a minute.
  • 2-2-2-2: 8-second rounds, a good place to start if holds make you uneasy.
  • Skip the empty hold: breathe in for 4, hold for 4, breathe out for 4, then go straight into the next inhale. Many people find the hold after the exhale the hardest part.

This matches both the research and the clinical advice. In the Stanford trial, box counts were personalized, from about 3 to 4 seconds up to 8 to 10 seconds, and participants were told to shorten them if they felt strained. Cleveland Clinic says to breathe gently, without straining, and notes that the counts can lengthen with practice. You can lengthen them over time if you enjoy it, but you don't have to.

If holds don't suit you at all, try calm 4-6 breathing: in for 4, out for 6, with no holds. Our guide to 4-6 breathing walks you through it. For a 3-3-3-3 or 2-2-2-2 box, the custom breathing timer lets you set your own pattern.

How often should you do box breathing?

Once or twice a day is a reasonable rhythm, plus any time you need it. Cleveland Clinic recommends one or two times a day regardless of how you feel, which keeps the technique familiar for when you need it.

The Stanford data also shows what a realistic habit looks like. Breathwork participants averaged 5.76 minutes a day on 19.6 of the 28 days. They missed some days, and their mood gains still grew with the number of days they practiced. So a few minutes on most days is a realistic target. The study didn't compare that with occasional longer sessions.

At bedtime, keep it gentle: shorter counts, a dim room, and a few minutes at most. Some people find the holds a little alerting at night and prefer a longer exhale instead. If scrolling is what keeps you up, doomscrolling at night covers that side of it. If you have ongoing trouble sleeping, talk to a doctor.

When to stop: dizziness and other safety notes

Box breathing is gentle for most people, but a few rules matter.

  • Stop if you feel dizzy or lightheaded. Go back to normal breathing and sit or lie down. Next time, shorten the counts or skip the hold after the exhale.
  • Keep it slow and soft. Don't force your breath or speed up the pattern.
  • Check with a clinician first if you're pregnant or have a heart or lung condition, seizures, glaucoma, a history of fainting, or panic that gets worse when you focus on your breathing.
  • Never hold your breath in or near water, or while driving.
  • Pause before tasks that need quick reactions, since reaction times may be slower right after a session.
  • It isn't a treatment. Box breathing can help you feel calmer, but it doesn't treat anxiety, panic or insomnia. If stress or anxiety is persistent or getting in the way of your life, talk to a professional. If you're in crisis, call or text 988 in the US, or contact your local emergency services.

item.title: Nervous System Overload From Your Phone: How to Come Down Mid-Scroll
item.description: Nervous system overload from your phone: why scrolling leaves you wired, what research shows, and a 60-second script to calm down mid-scroll.
item.content:encoded:
Nervous system overload from your phone is a plain-language name (not a diagnosis) for the tense, wired-but-flat state that fast, emotionally charged feeds and constant alerts can leave you in. Early research suggests scrolling keeps your body quietly aroused, and stopping can bring a spike of stress. Slow breathing (for example 4 counts in, 6 out) is one of the better-supported ways down.

In short, the problem has less to do with how many minutes you spend and more to do with the state the feed leaves you in. You can work with that state directly, in the middle of a scroll, without deleting anything or shutting yourself out.

What is nervous system overload from your phone?

Nervous system overload from your phone describes how your body feels after a stretch of scrolling that was supposed to be relaxing: switched on and oddly drained at the same time. It isn't a medical term, and having it doesn't mean something is wrong with you.

The felt signs tend to be physical before they are mental:

  • A tight jaw, or back teeth pressed together
  • Shoulders creeping up toward your ears
  • A buzzy head that won't settle on one thing
  • A shorter fuse with the people around you
  • Trouble settling into the next task, or into sleep

Your autonomic nervous system has two broad branches that work together all day. The sympathetic side revs you up for action. The parasympathetic side, which includes the vagus nerve, helps you settle and recover. Neither one is "bad," and you are never running purely on one of them.

Lots of articles say phones keep you "stuck in fight or flight." It's a tidy story, but the research is messier than that. What the evidence actually suggests is more interesting, and more useful.

It also helps to think of this as a state, not a score. Two people can spend the same 20 minutes on the same app and come away feeling completely different, depending on what they saw, how fast it moved, and what pinged in the middle. You don't need to think of yourself as having a problem to notice that some sessions leave you rattled.

Why does "one quick check" leave you wired?

"One quick check" tends to leave you wired because a feed packs dozens of small jolts into a few minutes: rapid topic switches, constant novelty, emotionally loaded posts, and notification interruptions. None of them is a big deal on its own. They add up.

Picture a typical two minutes. A friend's holiday photo, a clip about a disaster, a joke, an argument in the comments, an ad, then a message alert that pulls you into another app. Your attention and your emotions get pulled somewhere new every few seconds, and you rarely get to finish one feeling before the next one starts.

What you're looking at matters too. In a survey of 800 university students in Iran and the US, doomscrolling was associated with higher existential anxiety. That was a cross-sectional study, so it shows a link and doesn't prove that doomscrolling causes anxiety. Still, it matches something most people already know: five minutes of bleak headlines lands differently from five minutes of dog videos.

That is why minutes alone are a blunt measure. Pace, emotional tone and interruptions all shape how you feel afterward, not just the clock. If evenings are when this hits hardest, our piece on why doomscrolling at night leaves you wired goes deeper on that window.

What happens in your body while you scroll, and when you stop

A small Durham University lab study found that scrolling Instagram lowered heart rate while raising skin conductance, a common marker of arousal, and that stopping pushed both up along with stress. Put simply, you can seem absorbed and still while you scroll, then feel edgy the moment you put the phone down.

Here are the details. Researchers had 54 young adults use Instagram for 15 minutes. Compared with a baseline reading task, heart rate went down and skin conductance went up. Skin conductance tracks tiny changes in sweat gland activity, which is why researchers use it as a sign of physiological arousal. So the picture during scrolling wasn't panic. It was closer to absorbed and quietly switched on at the same time.

The more striking part came afterward. When participants stopped, their heart rate and skin conductance rose, and they reported stress, anxiety and craving. As one of the researchers described it, skin conductance climbed further when the session was interrupted.

That maps neatly onto the "wired but flat" feeling. While you scroll, you're absorbed and physically still. When you stop, there's a small surge, and you look up at your kitchen with a tight jaw and an itch to pick the phone back up.

There are two important caveats:

  • This isn't about addiction. The physiological pattern was not associated with participants' problematic-use scores, so it showed up in ordinary users and not only heavy ones. The author does not conclude that everyone is addicted, and says it is unclear whether the log-off response is withdrawal.
  • It's one small study. Fifty-four young adults, one app, in a lab. It's a useful clue, not a settled fact.

The practical point is that the moment you stop scrolling is a pressure point of its own, and a short reset there can help.

Do notifications and fast-switching feeds make it worse?

Notifications seem to add to the load, but cutting them off completely isn't automatically better. The best available evidence favors batching alerts over silencing everything.

In a study of 221 people, participants reported more inattention and hyperactivity during a week with phone alerts on than during a week with them off, and that inattention predicted lower well-being. The study relied on self-report and doesn't show that phones cause ADHD. What it does suggest is that a steady trickle of pings makes it harder to feel settled.

A later field experiment adds an important twist. In a 237-person study, getting notifications in batches three times a day improved mood and lowered stress, while getting no notifications at all raised anxiety and fear of missing out. It's a single experiment, so treat it as a strong hint rather than a rule.

That second finding matters. Switching every alert off can backfire, because worrying about what you're missing turns into its own source of tension. Fewer, predictable interruptions seem to work better than none.

Does hunching over your phone change how you breathe?

Possibly, but the evidence is thin. One small study found heavier phone users had more forward head posture and weaker forceful exhales, while other lung measures didn't differ significantly.

In a study of 50 people, those who used a smartphone more than 4 hours a day had more forward head posture and lower peak expiratory flow, but their forced vital capacity and FEV1 did not differ significantly. Peak expiratory flow measures how hard you can blow out, not how you breathe at rest, so it tells us little about breathing while you scroll.

You might notice something for yourself, though: shallow, upper-chest breathing when you're hunched and absorbed, or holding your breath while you read something tense. That's worth paying attention to. Just treat it as something you observe in yourself, not an established mechanism. We're skipping the catchy labels here, because the research hasn't caught up with them.

How to calm down when you're overstimulated mid-scroll

The best time to calm down is mid-scroll, right when you notice you're wound up, not at a gate before you open the app. That's when the overstimulated feeling is actually there. And the Durham findings suggest the comedown, when you stop, is when stress tends to rise.

A pause before you open an app catches you at a moment when you're usually fine. A mid-scroll pause catches you when you aren't.

The 60-second script

  1. Notice and name it. Say it in your head: "I'm wound up." Naming the state is your cue to switch, and it keeps the reset from feeling like a punishment.
  2. Drop your shoulders. Lift them slightly toward your ears, then let them fall. Let your arms feel heavy.
  3. Unclench your jaw. Let your back teeth part a little. Your lips can stay closed, with your tongue resting softly in your mouth.
  4. Widen your gaze. Look up from the screen and take in the edges of the room (the walls, the window, the ceiling) without focusing hard on anything.
  5. Breathe in for 4, out for 6. Inhale gently through your nose for a count of 4, then breathe out slowly for a count of 6. Each breath takes about 10 seconds.
  6. Repeat for six breaths. Six breaths of 4 in and 6 out takes one minute, which works out to six breaths per minute. Then decide on purpose whether to keep scrolling.

Steps 2 to 4 take a few seconds, so fold them into your first breath or two. If you'd like a pacer, the calm 4-6 breathing timer counts for you, and our guide to 4-6 breathing covers variations and how to adjust the counts.

What it feels like, and common mistakes

The first two breaths usually feel a little awkward. By the fourth or fifth, many people find their shoulders have dropped further on their own and their head has gone quieter. You're not aiming for bliss. You're aiming to come down a notch.

Common mistakes:

  • Forcing the exhale. Six counts should feel like a slow leak, not a push. If you run out of air early, count a bit faster.
  • Overfilling your lungs. A 4-count inhale is a normal-sized breath, not a gulp.
  • Checking the feed between breaths. One glance restarts the whole cycle. Turn the phone face down for the minute.
  • Treating it like a test. If you lose count, pick it up again at the next inhale.

If focusing on your breath feels worse

Some people find that focusing on their breath makes them more anxious. If that's you, skip the counting. Keep your eyes open, breathe normally, and just do the body steps: shoulders, jaw, gaze. If you feel dizzy, lightheaded, tingly or short of breath at any point, stop and go back to breathing normally.

This mid-scroll moment is exactly what DeRot is built for. It pauses your scroll after the feed has wound you up and walks you through a 60-second breath, so your shoulders drop and the wired feeling fades before you carry on. DeRot is coming soon to iOS.

What the research supports, and where it's still early

There's strong evidence that slow breathing raises vagally mediated heart rate variability. Whether a longer exhale beats an even breath is less clear, and the body cues in the script (shoulders, jaw, gaze) haven't been tested. They're simply easy ways to let go of tension.

Heart rate variability (HRV) is the natural beat-to-beat variation in your heart rate. Some HRV measures, such as RMSSD and high-frequency HRV, reflect activity of the vagus nerve, the main parasympathetic "settling" pathway.

Here is what the studies show:

  • Slow breathing and HRV. A meta-analysis of 223 studies found slow breathing increased vagally mediated HRV during a session, immediately after a single session, and after multi-session practice.
  • Six breaths per minute. Slow breathing at six cycles per minute raised RMSSD from before to after practice, with or without HRV biofeedback. The one-minute version above is shorter than the sessions typically studied. Treat it as a quick reset, and take a few minutes when you can.
  • Longer exhale. In a study of 28 adults, breathing out longer than breathing in, at the same overall rate, acutely increased RMSSD and high-frequency HRV, and high-frequency HRV stayed elevated for about 4 minutes afterward. That's encouraging, but it's one small study, and researchers haven't settled whether exhale length matters as much as simply slowing down. Use 4-6 because it's comfortable, not because it's proven to be better.
  • Mood without HRV change. In a month-long randomized trial, 5 minutes a day of cyclic sighing improved mood and lowered breathing rate more than mindfulness meditation. According to a summary of the trial, there was no significant change in HRV, and most of the 108 participants were Stanford undergraduates, so the results may not apply to everyone. It's also a useful reminder that feeling better and moving an HRV number aren't the same thing.
Claim Evidence strength Source
Slow breathing raises vagally mediated HRV Strong: meta-analysis of 223 studies Laborde 2022
Six breaths per minute raises RMSSD, with or without biofeedback Moderate: one lab study, before-and-after change Laborde 2021
A longer exhale adds extra benefit Early and mixed: small studies Bae 2021
Daily breathwork improves mood Promising: one month-long trial, mostly students Balban 2023
Scrolling raises arousal and stopping spikes stress Early: one lab study of 54 Wadsley and Ihssen (Durham)
Phone posture changes breathing Thin: 50 people, one measure differed Jung 2016
Dropping shoulders, unclenching jaw, widening gaze Untested: simple comfort cues None

None of this turns a breathing exercise into medical care for anxiety or any other condition. Slow breathing is associated with higher vagal HRV, and it may help you feel calmer in the moment. That's a worthwhile, modest claim, and we'd rather make that one honestly than a bigger one we can't back up.

Regulate, don't restrict: staying connected without the overstimulation tax

"Regulate, don't restrict" means dealing with the state your phone leaves you in instead of deleting apps or shutting yourself out. You can keep the group chat, the news and the funny videos, and still stop paying the overstimulation tax.

Two moves have the best support:

  • Batch your notifications into a few set times a day instead of switching everything off. In the 237-person experiment above, three batches a day beat both constant alerts and none at all. On an iPhone, go to Settings > Notifications > Scheduled Summary, switch it on, choose which apps to include, and set two or three delivery times. Calls, messages from people and time-sensitive alerts can still come through right away.
  • Take a breathable pause when you notice you're wired. Run the 60-second script mid-scroll, then decide whether to keep going.

If you'd like other options, the physiological sigh (two inhales through the nose, then a long, slow exhale) and box breathing are both worth trying. A safety note: breath holds and more forceful patterns, including box breathing, 4-7-8 and the physiological sigh, aren't for everyone. Take care if you're pregnant, have a heart or lung condition, or have a history of fainting or panic. Gentle 4-6 breathing, or ordinary breathing with soft shoulders, is a fine place to stay.

When to talk to a professional

A breathing reset is for everyday overstimulation, and it doesn't replace care. If jaw clenching, headaches or neck pain keep coming back, see a dentist, doctor or physiotherapist. If anxiety, sleep problems or distress persist, talk to a professional. If you're in crisis, contact local emergency services, or call or text 988 in the US.

For everyone else, the point is a small one: you don't have to give up the feed to stop leaving it frazzled. Notice the state, come down a notch, and carry on.

item.title: Is Scrolling Before Bed Bad? What Matters More Than Blue Light
item.description: Is scrolling before bed bad? Blue light is often a smaller factor than you've heard. See what the research says, and a 10-second test to check yourself.
item.content:encoded:
Scrolling before bed isn't automatically bad for sleep. For most adults, the blue light from a phone is probably a smaller factor than the headlines suggest. What tends to matter more is how much later the "one more" loop pushes your bedtime, and how wound up you feel when you finally put the phone down.

Most advice skips that last part. Two people can scroll for the same 30 minutes and have very different nights. One drifts off. The other lies there with a busy head and a tight jaw. The minutes matter less than the state you're in when you stop.

Is scrolling before bed bad? What the experts actually agree on

Researchers agree about children and teenagers, and they don't agree about adults. In 2024, a panel of 16 experts reviewed more than 2,200 articles on screens and sleep and reached consensus that screens and the content on them impair sleep in children and adolescents. They did not reach consensus on whether screen light impairs sleep for anyone, or on whether screen time, light or content affects adults.

That's worth sitting with, given how confidently most articles open with "yes, it's bad."

One of the largest recent studies of young adults points somewhere more specific. In a 2025 study of 45,202 students aged 18 to 28, each extra hour of screen use after going to bed was linked to 59% higher odds of insomnia symptoms and about 24 fewer minutes of sleep. Social media was no worse than other things people did on screens in bed. Total time in bed with a screen mattered more than the app.

That study is cross-sectional, a single snapshot, so it can't show which way the arrow points. Still, it nudges the useful question away from "is my phone bad for me?" and toward "what is my scroll doing to me tonight?"

Three ways a bedtime scroll can affect sleep

A bedtime scroll can affect your sleep in three different ways: through the light from the screen, by pushing your bedtime later, or by leaving your mind and body activated. Each has its own evidence, and most articles blend them together. Pulling them apart tells you which one, if any, applies to you.

Mechanism What it does Evidence in adults What helps
Light Screen light can suppress melatonin and nudge your body clock later Real in lab studies, usually modest at normal phone brightness; sensitivity varies a lot Lower brightness, dim room lights; night mode helps only a little
Bedtime displacement "One more" pushes sleep later, so you get less of it Consistent links with shorter sleep, mostly from snapshot surveys A rough stop time; phone charging across the room
Arousal Charged content keeps your mind busy and your body activated Plausible and expert-backed, but no formal consensus Gentler content; a slow-exhale breath before you settle

Does blue light from your phone really suppress melatonin?

Yes, bright evening light, including screen light, can suppress melatonin, the hormone that rises in the evening as your body gets ready for sleep. The real question is how much a phone at ordinary brightness does, and for most adults the answer seems to be "some, but less than you've heard."

The study behind many headlines is a 2015 lab experiment in which 12 adults read on a light-emitting eReader for four hours a night, five nights in a row. Compared with reading a printed book, melatonin was suppressed by 55%, its evening rise came more than 1.5 hours later, and falling asleep took about 10 minutes longer (25.7 versus 15.8 minutes). Those are real effects. They also came from four hours of reading in a dim lab, night after night, which isn't how most people use a phone.

A closer match to everyday life: a 2024 study found that 90 minutes of reading on a smartphone lowered melatonin, but whole-night sleep was largely unaffected. The adults in that study had a little less deep sleep early in the night, and that was about it. It included only males aged 14 to 25, so it doesn't settle the question for everyone.

Brightness is part of the story. Stanford sleep researcher Jamie Zeitzer estimates that a phone at night gives off roughly 25 to 50 lux, compared with 10,000 to 100,000 lux from sunlight.

Why "it's probably fine" isn't the whole answer

People differ a lot in how sensitive they are to evening light. In a 2019 study of 55 adults, melatonin was half-suppressed at about 25 lux on average, but individual sensitivity ranged from 6 to 350 lux, a more than 50-fold difference. That study used room lighting, not phones, so it doesn't translate directly. What it does show is that an "average" effect hides a wide spread. Screen light may barely register for one person and matter more for another.

So blue light isn't nothing. For most adults it's just unlikely to be the main event.

Does night mode or Night Shift help you sleep?

Night mode probably does little for sleep on its own. In a 2021 BYU study of 167 adults aged 18 to 24, sleep did not differ between people who used their phone with Night Shift on, with Night Shift off, or who didn't use a phone at all in the hour before bed. The BYU researchers pointed to psychological stimulation as a separate factor, one a warmer tint can't touch.

A small University of Salzburg pilot of 14 people found that blue-light filters only partly softened the effects of evening smartphone light.

The verdict: if you like the warmer screen, leave night mode on. It's harmless. Just don't count on it to fix a bad night. The same goes for blue-light glasses: none of the studies here tested them, and we wouldn't spend money expecting them to change your sleep. If you suspect you're light-sensitive, turning the brightness down and keeping room lights low is simpler.

The bigger factor: "one more" and a later bedtime

For many people, the main cost of a bedtime scroll is time. You pick up the phone at 10:40 to check one thing, and the next time you look at the clock it's 11:55. In the 2025 student study, each extra hour of screen use after going to bed went with about 24 fewer minutes of sleep.

Researchers call this bedtime procrastination: putting off sleep without a real reason to stay up. In a 2024 study of 245 adolescents, bedtime procrastination helped explain the link between problematic phone use and poor sleep quality. That study was of teenagers and was cross-sectional, so treat it as a plausible mechanism for adults rather than proof.

There's also a direction problem. Snapshot studies measure everything at once, so poor sleepers may reach for the phone because they can't sleep, not only the other way around. If you've ever lain awake and picked up your phone out of restlessness, you know that loop from the inside.

Why some content leaves you wired

What you scroll may matter more than the light it's shown on. Zeitzer argues that emotionally activating content probably matters more than screen light. Some people use soothing videos to wind down, though he cautions that even positive content can be stimulating. Sleep experts at Singapore General Hospital make a similar point: how long you use the phone near bedtime and how emotionally stimulating the content is matter more in delaying sleep.

Think about what a typical feed serves up in five minutes: a friend's baby photo, a heated argument in the comments, a work message, a news alert, a clip that makes you laugh out loud. Each one asks your nervous system to respond. Your heart runs a little quicker, your jaw sets, your thoughts start replaying the reply you didn't write. That's arousal in the physiological sense, and it's close to the opposite of the slow, heavy settling that sleep needs.

To be honest about the evidence: this explanation is plausible and backed by experts, but the 2024 panel found no consensus on content and adult sleep either. Treat it as a strong hunch you can test against your own nights. For more on this pattern, see why doomscrolling at night leaves you wired.

Why you fall asleep fine some nights and lie awake on others

Sleep pressure explains a lot of it. The longer you've been awake and the more tired you are, the stronger your drive to sleep. BYU researcher Chad Jensen summed it up this way: when you're very tired, you fall asleep regardless of what you did on your phone.

So after a long, draining day, a 30-minute scroll may cost you almost nothing. On a night when you're less tired, or when the feed served up something that got under your skin, the same habit can leave you staring at the ceiling.

Two other things move from night to night. Your sensitivity to light is your own (and it varies widely between people), and what you happened to see changes every time you open the app. Inconsistent nights don't mean you're doing something wrong. They mean the scroll is one input among several.

The drowsy-or-wired test

The most useful data point is how you feel in the moment you put the phone down. Next time, before you roll over, take ten seconds and notice:

  • Eyelids: heavy, or wide open?
  • Jaw and shoulders: soft, or held?
  • Thoughts: drifting, or replaying something you read?
  • Heart: slow and unremarkable, or a little quick?

If you're drowsy, the scroll is probably harmless, or its main cost is time. If you're waking up short on sleep, the thing to change is when you stop, not whether you scroll. Try a rough stop time for a week and see whether you wake up better rested.

If you're wired, arousal is the likely issue, and night mode won't touch it. What helps is changing what you look at in the last stretch (some people do fine with familiar, low-stakes content), stopping earlier, or bringing your body down before you try to sleep. If what you watch leaves you distressed or excited, Zeitzer suggests putting the phone down about an hour before bed. That's expert advice rather than a tested cutoff, so treat it as a starting point you can adjust.

Run the check for a week. Many people find a pattern quickly: one app, one topic, or one kind of late-night thread that reliably leaves them buzzing, while other scrolling barely registers.

If you're wired: a slow-exhale breath to come down

A slow breath with a longer exhale is a simple way to come down from a wired scroll. Calm 4-6 breathing means breathing in for a count of 4 and out for a count of 6, which works out to about six breaths per minute. One minute is six breaths.

  1. Put the phone face down on the nightstand.
  2. Breathe in gently through your nose for a count of 4, letting your belly rise.
  3. Breathe out slowly through your nose or softly parted lips for a count of 6.
  4. Repeat for about 60 seconds, roughly six breaths.
  5. Check again: jaw, shoulders, thoughts. Notice whether anything has softened.

If counting in the dark is annoying, the calm 4-6 breathing timer paces it for you. For more detail on technique and common mistakes, see how to do 4-6 breathing in 60 seconds.

What the evidence does and doesn't show

The most relevant trial is encouraging. In a 2019 randomized trial with 64 participants analyzed, 15 minutes of slow breathing at about six breaths per minute each evening for 30 days improved self-reported sleep quality and overnight vagal activity (a marker of the nervous system's calming branch). A comparison group that spent the same 15 minutes on social media saw no change. That was 15 minutes a night for a month, though. A 60-second version is less tested.

A 2020 pilot of 20 young adults found that 30 minutes of slow breathing before bed raised heart rate variability right away but had no robust effect on sleep measured in the lab. The honest summary: slow breathing can help you feel calmer in the moment, which may make settling easier. It isn't a sleep treatment.

That mid-scroll moment, when you notice you're wound up but still holding the phone, is what DeRot is being built for. It meets you mid-scroll and walks you through a minute of breathing, so you put the phone down with your shoulders lower and your head quieter. It's coming soon to iOS. For a fuller wind-down routine, see the night doomscrolling guide, and browse more in sleep and winding down.

A few safety notes

Keep the breathing gentle. If you feel dizzy or lightheaded, stop and breathe normally. The 4-6 pattern has no breath holds, but if you're pregnant, have a heart or lung condition, or have a history of fainting or panic, skip breath holds and fast breathing and check with your doctor before trying new techniques.

Changing your phone habits or your breathing won't treat insomnia. If poor sleep happens most nights for several weeks, or it's affecting your days, talk to a doctor or sleep specialist. If the wired feeling is really recurring anxiety or distress, a professional can help. If you might be in crisis, contact local emergency services, or call or text 988 in the US.

item.title: 4-6 Breathing: How to Do the Calm Pattern in 60 Seconds
item.description: 4-6 breathing means in for 4, out for 6, no holds, about 6 breaths a minute. Clear steps, a 60-second mid-scroll script, common mistakes and safety tips.
item.content:encoded:
4-6 breathing is a slow breathing pattern in which you breathe in through your nose for 4 counts and out for 6, with no breath holds. Each breath takes about 10 seconds, so you breathe about 6 times a minute. Six breaths is roughly one minute, which makes it an easy reset right in the middle of a scroll.

It's the pattern to reach for when you surface from a feed with your shoulders up and your head buzzing: nothing to hold, nothing complicated to count, just a slightly longer out-breath than in-breath.

What is 4-6 breathing?

4-6 breathing (sometimes written 4:6, or called extended exhale breathing) is a no-hold pattern: in for a count of 4, out for a count of 6, then straight into the next breath. At roughly one count per second, a full breath takes 10 seconds and the pace lands at about 6 breaths per minute.

That pace is the useful part. Six breaths take about a minute, which fits into the gap between noticing you're wound up and deciding what to do next. A UK mental health guide, Breathing Out Anxiety, recommends exactly this pattern: in for 4, out for 6, without holding your breath.

A few similar names cause confusion:

  • 4-4-6 and 4-2-6 keep the longer out-breath but add a hold of 4 or 2 counts after the inhale. That slows the pace further and gives you one more thing to count.
  • Coherent or resonance breathing (often 5-5) runs at about the same pace, roughly 6 breaths a minute, but the in-breath and out-breath are equal.
  • 4-7-8 is a different pattern entirely, built around a long 7-count hold.

If you'd rather not count in your head, the free calm 4-6 breathing timer paces each breath for you.

How to do 4-6 breathing, step by step

To do 4-6 breathing, breathe in gently through your nose for 4 counts, then breathe out slowly for 6 counts with no pause in between, and repeat for 6 breaths. Here is the full version:

  1. Get settled. Sit or stand with your shoulders loose and your hands resting. Sit while you're learning, in case you feel lightheaded.
  2. Breathe in softly through your nose for 4. Fill to about 70-80% of a full breath, not to the brim. Let your belly and lower ribs widen rather than lifting your shoulders.
  3. With no pause at the top, breathe out slowly for 6. Use your nose or softly pursed lips, as if cooling a spoonful of soup. Let the air leave; don't squeeze it out.
  4. Let the next inhale start on its own. There may be a tiny natural turnaround at the bottom. Don't turn it into a hold.
  5. Repeat for 6 breaths. That's about one minute.

Count at roughly one per second. "One-and, two-and" is a reliable way to stop the count from speeding up.

Nose or mouth?

Breathe in through your nose; it's quieter and makes a slow inhale easier to control. Breathe out through either. Pursed lips make it easier to stretch the exhale to 6, while breathing out through the nose is less noticeable on a train or in an office.

A 60-second 4-6 breathing script for mid-scroll

The best moment for 4-6 breathing is partway through the feed, when you notice your jaw is set, your shoulders have crept up, or you feel a hum of irritation or a slightly sped-up, wired feeling. You don't have to close the app or decide anything yet. Put the phone face down on your knee, or just look away from the screen.

Breath 1 (0-10 seconds). In, 2, 3, 4. Out, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Just slow down. If the count wobbles, let it. No judging.

Breaths 2-3 (10-30 seconds). Keep the same count. On each out-breath, let your shoulders drop a little. Don't place them; let them fall.

Breaths 4-5 (30-50 seconds). On the out-breath, unclench your jaw: teeth slightly apart, tongue resting. Soften your eyes and let your gaze widen to the room.

Breath 6 (50-60 seconds). Notice what changed, even if it's small. Then decide on purpose: go back to the feed, answer the message, or put the phone down.

The goal here is your state, not your screen time. You're not trying to log off or earn a streak. If you go back to scrolling a notch calmer, that counts. (If this happens to you mostly in bed, our guide to doomscrolling at night covers that moment specifically.)

This mid-scroll minute is what DeRot is built around. It pauses your scroll after the feed has wound you up and walks you through a minute of Calm breathing (in 4, out 6), so your shoulders drop and the wired feeling fades before you carry on. It's coming soon to iOS; until then, the free timer does the counting.

What 4-6 breathing feels like (and what it shouldn't)

Done comfortably, 4-6 breathing usually feels like a gradual settling: your breath gets quieter, your shoulders come down, your jaw loosens and the buzzy edge eases over a minute or so. These are common experiences, not guarantees. Some days you'll notice a lot, some days very little, and both are normal.

It shouldn't feel like a strain. Watch for:

  • Air hunger, the sense that you're not getting enough air
  • Gasping or grabbing at the next inhale
  • Tingling in your fingers or lips
  • Lightheadedness or chest discomfort

Any of these means the counts are too long or the breaths too big. Shorten to 3-5, or stop and breathe normally.

Common 4-6 breathing mistakes

Most 4-6 breathing mistakes come from trying too hard. The pattern works best when it feels slightly lazy.

  • Gulping the inhale. Filling to the brim in 4 counts makes the breath sharp. Sip in to about 70-80% instead.
  • Pushing the exhale. Forcing the air out tenses your belly and throat. Let the breath leave slowly, like a tyre with a slow leak.
  • Counting too fast. If your 4-and-6 takes 6 seconds instead of 10, you're at about 10 breaths a minute, right at the cutoff of what researchers define as slow breathing (fewer than 10 a minute). Check against a timer once to calibrate.
  • Lifting the shoulders. Chest-and-shoulder breathing works against the point. Let the belly and lower ribs do the moving.
  • Holding at the top out of habit. If you usually do box or 4-7-8, you may pause automatically. Turn straight from in to out.
  • Big open-mouth sighs. One sigh is fine. Several deep, fast ones in a row can tip you into over-breathing, which is often what causes tingling.
  • Getting perfectionist about the count. If counting makes you tense, drop the numbers. Just make each out-breath a little longer than the in-breath.

What if 6 seconds feels too long? Try 3-5 first

If a 6-count exhale leaves you short of air, keep the shape and shorten the counts: in for 3, out for 5. That's 8 seconds per breath, or about 7 to 8 breaths a minute, which is still slow breathing.

A gentle progression looks like this:

  1. 3-5 until it feels easy
  2. 4-6, the standard pattern
  3. 5-7 (about 5 breaths a minute), optional, only if 4-6 starts to feel effortless

You can set any of these on the custom breathing timer. Comfort beats hitting exact numbers. A relaxed 3-5 does more for you than a strained 4-6.

4-6 breathing vs 4-7-8 vs box breathing: which is gentler?

For most people, 4-6 breathing is the gentlest of the common patterns because it has no breath holds. There's nothing to hold through and only two numbers to track, which suits people who find holds uncomfortable or who get a little panicky when air is "stopped."

The table below is our practical guide, not study data: the breaths-per-minute figures are simple arithmetic at one count per second, and the difficulty and dizziness ratings reflect how these patterns tend to feel.

Pattern Holds Breaths per minute (approx.) Difficulty Dizziness risk Best moment
4-6 (calm) None 6 Easy Low, if the inhale stays soft Mid-scroll, any time you feel wound up
Box (4-4-4-4) Two 4-count holds 3.75 Moderate Low to moderate When you want something structured to focus on
4-7-8 One 7-count hold About 3 Harder Moderate Winding down, sitting or lying
Physiological sigh None (double inhale, long exhale) Varies Easy Low for a few breaths; higher if rushed A quick reset of one to a few breaths

Holds aren't bad, and other patterns have real support. NHS inform's controlled breathing exercise uses a 3-3-3-3 pattern with holds. A 2023 study in Cell Reports Medicine found that daily 5-minute cyclic sighing improved mood and lowered respiratory rate more than mindfulness meditation over one month.

If you want to compare them yourself, try the box breathing timer, the 4-7-8 breathing timer or the physiological sigh guide.

Why does a longer exhale help? A short, honest summary

The honest answer is that the slow pace seems to do most of the work. A longer exhale may add to how relaxed you feel, but it hasn't shown a clear extra benefit over equal in and out breaths.

The case for slow breathing is fairly solid. A review of 15 studies found that breathing at under 10 breaths a minute was associated with higher heart rate variability (HRV) and more comfort and relaxation, though the evidence base was small. A larger meta-analysis of 223 studies found that vagally mediated HRV rose during slow breathing, right after a single session, and after multi-session practice.

The exhale ratio is more mixed:

  • In a study of 30 people, a long exhale produced more self-reported relaxation and less stress than a long inhale, with an HRV gain that appeared only at 6 breaths a minute.
  • In a randomised trial with 94 adults analysed, anxiety fell in both the longer-exhale and equal-breathing groups, with no significant difference between them.
  • A comparison of 1:1 and 1:2 breathing at 6 breaths a minute (26 people, plus a replication with 16) found no difference in HRV.
  • One study even found an HRV advantage for equal breathing at 5.5 breaths a minute.

The usual explanation involves the vagus nerve and the rest-and-digest side of the nervous system. It's plausible and partly supported, but not settled. Practically: slow down first, and use the longer exhale because it feels good, not because it's magic.

How long should you do 4-6 breathing?

One minute, or six breaths, is enough for a mid-scroll reset. It's short enough to actually do and long enough to notice a shift.

If you want a longer practice, the NHS suggests repeating calming breathing for at least 5 minutes and notes it can be done anywhere, and the PPT guide suggests building up gradually to 10 minutes.

Keep expectations proportional. A meta-analysis of breathwork trials found a small-to-medium reduction in stress (12 RCTs, 785 adults), with most studies at moderate risk of bias. That's encouraging, and still developing.

A quick safety note

4-6 breathing is gentle, but stop and go back to normal breathing if you feel dizzy, lightheaded, tingly or short of air, or have any chest discomfort. Sit or lie down while you're learning. If you're pregnant, have a heart or lung condition, or have a history of fainting or panic attacks, check with a clinician before making any breathing practice a regular habit.

Breathing can help you feel calmer and may reduce stress, but it doesn't treat anxiety, panic or insomnia. If anxiety, distress or sleep problems keep coming back, talk to a professional. If you're in crisis, call 988 in the US or your local emergency services.

item.title: Doomscrolling at Night: Why You're Wired and a 60-Second Way Down
item.description: Doomscrolling at night leaves you wired, not sleepy. Here's why, plus a 60-second breathing script to use in bed with the phone still in hand.
item.content:encoded:
Doomscrolling at night winds your body up just when you meant to wind down. You can take the edge off in about 60 seconds without getting out of bed. Breathe in through your nose for 4 and out slowly for 6, five or six times (or do two or three physiological sighs), then turn the phone face down.

You probably know how this goes. You got into bed, picked up the phone to check one thing, and came up half an hour later with a tight jaw and a slightly quick heartbeat. Sleep felt further away than when you started.

Most advice on this starts with rules: keep the phone out of the bedroom, or stop at a hard cutoff time. Those work for some people. This guide starts with how the scroll leaves you feeling. The number of minutes matters less than the state you end up in, and you can change that state tonight.

What to do if you're doomscrolling at night right now

Stop on whatever post is on screen and give yourself one minute of slow breathing with an exhale longer than the inhale. Then turn the phone face down. You don't need a new rule or a resolution. Just change where your body is heading.

Here is the short version:

  1. Let your thumb go still. You don't need to close the app.
  2. Breathe in through your nose for 4, then out slowly for 6. Do this five or six times.
  3. Turn the phone face down and let one more slow exhale be the end of the day.

The full script, what it should feel like, and the mistakes that cancel it out are further down. First, it helps to know why the feed revs you up at all.

Why scrolling in bed leaves you wired instead of sleepy

Late-night feeds are built to hold your attention, and the content that holds attention best often keeps your mind active, which is the opposite of what sleep needs. The problem is less about time on the screen and more about how emotionally involved the screen makes you.

Bad news is sticky

Susan Tapert, a professor of psychiatry at UC San Diego, puts it plainly: "Bad news grabs and holds our attention more strongly than good news ..." Alarming headlines engage the brain's threat detection. That is useful when there is something to deal with and much less useful at 11:40 pm with the lights off.

How invested you are matters more than how long you scroll

A 2024 study of 830 young adults found that frequent checking and emotional investment in social media predicted poor sleep more strongly than total screen time. Pre-sleep cognitive arousal (a busy, revved-up mind) and social comparison helped explain the link. That is the state-over-minutes idea in data form. As an illustration rather than a study result, ten minutes in a heated comment thread may leave you more wound up than forty minutes of cooking videos.

An earlier survey of 1,763 US young adults proposed three routes from social media to poor sleep: mental activation, a later bedtime, and screen light. Like most research in this area, it was cross-sectional, so it shows associations rather than proving cause.

The "one more" loop

Getting into bed is not the same thing as trying to sleep. In a study of 338 young adults, researchers found an average gap of about 39 minutes between going to bed and trying to sleep, linked to evening media use. An infinite feed never gives you a natural place to stop, so the stopping point has to come from you, at the end of the day when you're most tired.

Is it the blue light or the content keeping you awake?

Both can play a part, but for ordinary scrolling, blue light probably gets more blame than the evidence supports. The best-known study found an effect that was real, though modest, and it took a heavy dose.

In that 2015 study, 12 adults who read on an iPad for about four hours before bed on five evenings took nearly 10 minutes longer to fall asleep than when they read a printed book. They also showed suppressed melatonin, a delayed body clock, and lower alertness the next morning. Those findings are worth taking seriously. They also came from four hours of reading a night in a lab, which is a long way from a typical scroll.

Given the emotional-investment findings above, our reading is that what you look at probably matters at least as much as the light it comes through. That is an inference. The studies here weren't designed to settle it. Night mode or a warmer screen is a reasonable thing to keep on, though the evidence on night mode specifically is limited, and it won't touch the wired feeling you get from a news alert or a friend's highlight reel.

The 60-second off-ramp: a breathing script to use in bed, phone in hand

The off-ramp is one minute of slow breathing where the exhale is longer than the inhale. You do it right where you are, then put the phone face down. There are two versions, and both skip breath holds. Pick whichever feels easier tonight.

Option A: Calm 4-6 breathing

Calm 4-6 breathing is a slow-breathing pattern in which you inhale for 4 counts and exhale for 6, which comes to six breaths per minute.

  1. Stop scrolling and let your head sink into the pillow.
  2. Unclench your jaw and let your tongue rest loosely.
  3. Breathe in gently through your nose for a count of 4.
  4. Breathe out slowly for a count of 6, through your nose or softly through slightly parted lips, as if fogging a cool window.
  5. Repeat for five or six rounds. Each breath takes about 10 seconds, so six rounds is one minute.

If you'd like something to pace you, the free calm 4-6 breathing timer runs in your browser.

Option B: The physiological sigh

The physiological sigh is a breathing pattern in which you take a full inhale through the nose, top it up with a second short sip of air, then release it in a long, slow exhale through the mouth.

  1. Inhale through your nose until you feel comfortably full.
  2. Take one more short sip of air through the nose.
  3. Exhale slowly through your mouth, letting it last longer than both inhales together.
  4. Take two or three normal, easy breaths.
  5. Repeat for two or three sighs in total.

The physiological sigh timer walks you through the rhythm if counting in the dark feels like work.

Then: phone face down

After your last round, turn the phone face down on the nightstand and let one more slow exhale be the full stop. If you use the same small gesture every night, it can start to work as a cue that the day is over.

Why the longer exhale helps

Slow breathing under 10 breaths per minute is associated with increased heart rate variability, and a meta-analysis of 223 studies found that voluntary slow breathing increases vagally mediated heart rate variability, a marker tied to the vagus nerve and the body's rest-and-digest side. In a Stanford-led remote trial, 108 people did 5 minutes of breathwork or mindfulness a day for 28 days, and cyclic sighing was the only breathing practice that improved positive mood significantly more than mindfulness meditation. The breathwork groups also saw a bigger drop in respiratory rate than the mindfulness group.

Why not 4-7-8 or box breathing at bedtime?

Both include breath holds. For some people, holding the breath while already keyed up feels effortful or a little air-hungry, so we keep the bedtime script free of holds. That's a practical judgment on our part, not a study finding. Both techniques can still be useful at other times, and you'll find them with the other free breathing timers.

What it should feel like, and the most common mistakes

By the third or fourth round, the exhale should get easier to stretch out. Your shoulders settle into the mattress and your jaw softens. The itch for "one more" goes quiet. It should feel easy. Some nights the change is obvious, and some nights it's subtle, and both are normal.

The mistakes that undo it:

  • Forcing big breaths. What matters is the pace. Huge gulps can leave you lightheaded. Breathe at about the size of a normal breath, just slower.
  • Chaining sighs back to back. Take a few ordinary breaths between sighs.
  • Holding at the top. Let the inhale turn straight into the exhale.
  • Counting too fast. If 4-6 feels long, try 3-5. The key is keeping the exhale longer than the inhale.
  • Going straight back to the feed. Opening the same app again drops you right back where you started. Turn the phone over first and decide afterwards.

If you pick it back up anyway, that's fine. No guilt, no streak to break. Run the script again in ten minutes or tomorrow night. Each time you notice the wired feeling and do something about it, you're practising.

Does breathing help you fall asleep? What the evidence says

Slow breathing can help you feel calmer and less keyed up before bed, and people who practise it regularly often report sleeping better. The evidence that it objectively helps you fall asleep faster or sleep longer is still inconclusive.

A 2026 systematic review of 9 studies with 457 participants found that self-reported sleep improved in seven studies, most of which used 28 to 30 days of pre-bed slow breathing, while objective sleep results were inconclusive. The studies that measured sleep objectively tested only a single day of practice, so that question is still open. Six of the studies showed effects on heart rate variability. The Stanford trial matches that picture: mood improved and breathing rate came down, but there were no significant changes in heart rate variability, resting heart rate, or sleep over the month.

So treat the off-ramp as a way to come down from the feed, not as a sleeping pill. It helps you stop the climb, and sleep has a better chance from there.

Why you keep scrolling when you're exhausted

Revenge bedtime procrastination is staying up later than you meant to, often to claim some personal time after a day that felt like it belonged to everyone else. The phone is the easiest place to find that time, which is part of why it's so hard to put down.

That pull may be part of why the gap between getting into bed and trying to sleep stretches out, though the 39-minute study above didn't look at it directly. We'll cover it properly in a dedicated explainer soon. For now: wanting time of your own is reasonable. It just helps if that time doesn't leave you wound up.

Small evening setups that help (no hard cutoff required)

The aim of these setups is to put a little friction between you and the content that winds you up, without banning the phone. Choose one or two.

  • Charger across the room. You can still reach the phone. It just takes a few steps, and that's often enough to make you pause before picking it up.
  • Mute news and social alerts after a set time. Your phone's sleep or focus settings can do this automatically every night.
  • Move the charged apps off the home screen. In the evening, keep the apps that tend to wind you up a swipe or two further away.
  • Choose calmer content late. Since emotional investment tracks with poor sleep, a low-stakes hobby account or a long read is a better last stop than the news.
  • Make "face down" your ending ritual. Do the same gesture and the same slow exhale every night.

This mid-scroll moment is what DeRot is being built for. It meets you in the feed, pauses the scroll, and walks you through a 60-second breath so your shoulders drop and the wired feeling fades, and then you can carry on if you like. It's coming soon to iOS. There's more on why feeds leave you tense in our doomscrolling and scrolling stress hub.

When to talk to someone

Breathing is a low-risk way to feel calmer, but it's no substitute for care if you're dealing with insomnia, anxiety, or a heart condition. A few simple guardrails:

  • Stop if you feel dizzy, tingly, or lightheaded, and go back to normal breathing.
  • Keep it gentle and check with a clinician if you're pregnant, have a heart or lung condition, or have a history of fainting or panic. The Stanford trial excluded people with heart disease, glaucoma, seizures, or pregnancy, and about 10% of participants reported a negative experience.
  • See a doctor if your heart races often, or if a racing heart comes with chest pain, shortness of breath, or fainting.
  • Talk to a GP or mental health professional if trouble sleeping or anxiety keeps coming back.

If you're in distress or feel unsafe, contact local emergency services, or call or text 988 in the US.
